terms.definition: What it would cost to buy, as paid advertising, the same screen time a sponsor's marks earned inside a broadcast: qualified exposure seconds priced at that window's 30-second spot rate, then discounted roughly 25-50% because passive signage sells less than a commercial does.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-valuation roleplay asks whether a $400,000 rights fee paid off; you price the exposure seconds and apply the passive discount rather than quoting attendance.

terms.definition: The measurement rule that counts only branding a viewer could actually read — the logo must sit on screen unobstructed and in focus for at least one continuous second and fill a minimum share of the frame, or those seconds are struck from the valuation.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hand you an audit where gross on-screen time and qualified time differ by half; naming the threshold explains the gap instead of arguing the report is wrong.

terms.definition: How many dollars of promotional spending stand behind each dollar paid for the association itself; practice runs 1:1 at minimum and often 2:1, so a $500,000 rights fee needs another $500,000 to $1,000,000 before the partnership can work.
terms.whyItMatters: In a sponsorship-sale roleplay the client calls the fee affordable; you have to show the real budget is two to three times the fee or the signage sits unleveraged.

terms.definition: The uplift a property charges to lock every rival in one product class out of the venue, broadcast and apparel — the incremental fee less the revenue forgone by refusing the next-best buyer in that class, commonly 20-40% over the non-exclusive rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-pricing case gives you two soft-drink bidders; you must show exclusivity only pays when the premium beats what the excluded bidder would have spent.

terms.definition: Consideration delivered as goods, services or media instead of cash, credited against the rights fee at fair market value rather than list price — a $250,000 package carrying $100,000 of trade leaves $150,000 in cash, while the property books the trade at its own cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay sponsor offers product in place of money; the negotiation turns on valuing that trade at market before it may offset the fee.

terms.definition: Spreading a multi-year broadcast payment across the games actually telecast rather than evenly by calendar month, so a network carrying most of its schedule in one quarter recognizes most of that year's expense in that quarter.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-economics exam item asks why a broadcaster's fourth-quarter costs spike on a flat annual payment; the amortization pattern is the answer, not a fee increase.

terms.definition: A contract term barring a game's local telecast unless a stated condition is met — classically a sellout confirmed 72 hours before kickoff — inside a defined radius of the venue, shielding gate revenue from the broadcast of its own event.
terms.whyItMatters: A broadcast-rights roleplay asks whether to lift the local blackout; you weigh the walk-up ticket sales given up against the ratings and sponsor delivery the telecast adds.

terms.definition: Releasing one piece of content through exhibition channels in a fixed sequence, each protected by a contractual holdback of a set number of days before the next channel may carry it, with the price of each window falling as its exclusivity shortens.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-distribution roleplay asks about sending an event straight to streaming; the holdback lengths quantify the pay-per-view revenue that decision skips.

terms.definition: A network's promise that an advertiser's schedule will deliver a stated audience level, with any shortfall owed back in inventory computed as the guaranteed rating minus the delivered rating, multiplied by the units bought.
terms.whyItMatters: A sports-broadcast sales roleplay has a game under-deliver; you must state what the advertiser is owed and in what form before conceding a cash discount you do not owe.

terms.definition: The compensating commercial inventory issued when a guaranteed audience level is missed, valued at the original purchase rate rather than today's market rate and required to run in comparable dayparts so the replacement is genuinely equivalent.
terms.whyItMatters: When a rights-holder network under-delivers in a roleplay, the fight is over which daypart and which rate the replacement spots are valued at.

terms.definition: A per-subscriber monthly payment a distributor owes a broadcaster for carrying its signal: ten million subscribers at $2.50 each is $300 million a year, which is why a regional sports network is priced off subscriber count rather than ratings.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-rights case asks why a team's own channel is worth more than its advertising revenue suggests; the subscriber arithmetic carries the answer.

terms.definition: The licensee's payment computed on invoiced wholesale price after contractually allowed deductions — returns, freight and trade discounts, usually capped at a few percent — never on the retail shelf price, so 12% of a $30 wholesale unit is $3.60 and not $7.20.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandise-licensing roleplay quotes a rate without naming the base; pinning wholesale versus retail is the whole negotiation, because one percentage can pay double.

terms.definition: The upfront sum a licensor takes before any product ships is credited against royalties as they are earned, so a $100,000 advance at a 10% rate means the licensee owes nothing further until net sales pass $1,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: A licensing roleplay asks when the licensor next sees money; you compute the recoupment threshold instead of promising quarterly checks from day one.

terms.definition: Paid use of an amateur athlete's identity for endorsement, lawful only where it is genuine compensation for work rather than pay-for-play or a recruiting inducement, and reportable to the school — most policies require disclosure of any agreement at or above $600 within days of signing.
terms.whyItMatters: A collegiate-sponsorship roleplay dangles a booster-funded offer; the disclosure threshold and the inducement line decide whether you may sign it, not whether the athlete wants it.

terms.definition: A person's property interest in the commercial use of their identity, enforceable with no trademark or copyright behind it and surviving death in many states for a fixed term — seventy years in several — so an estate can still block an advertisement.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-licensing case puts a retired athlete's likeness on packaging; this doctrine and its post-mortem term are why clearance is required at all.

terms.definition: Royalties from products depicting several athletes are collected centrally and divided per unit among the players actually shown, so a card set featuring three athletes splits one royalty three ways rather than paying each of them a full rate.
terms.whyItMatters: A players-association roleplay asks how a team-wide trading-card deal pays out; the per-unit split, not individual star power, sets each athlete's check.

terms.definition: A termination right triggered by conduct bringing an endorser into public disrepute, where the drafted trigger decides everything: 'conviction' lets a brand act only after a verdict, while 'accusation' or 'public disrepute' lets it suspend payment on an allegation alone.
terms.whyItMatters: An endorsement-crisis roleplay hands you a headline with no charge filed; whether you may suspend the contract turns entirely on which trigger the clause uses.

terms.definition: Social-endorsement pricing benchmarked to audience size — roughly $10 per thousand followers per post, adjusted by measured engagement rate — so a 500,000-follower athlete posting at 3% engagement prices near $5,000, not at whatever the agent opens with.
terms.whyItMatters: An athlete-influencer negotiation roleplay starts from a number pulled out of the air; the follower-and-engagement math is how you defend or attack it.

terms.definition: A term stepping compensation up automatically once a defined objective achievement occurs — a major championship adding a set percentage to the annual retainer — as opposed to a bonus the brand may award at its own discretion.
terms.whyItMatters: A talent-contract roleplay tells you to hold the fee down; conceding an escalator rather than a higher base moves the cost into the year the win actually pays for.

terms.definition: The brand or studio owes the full contracted fee whether or not it ever uses the talent, unless it terminates inside a defined window before services begin — so shelving a campaign is a budgeting decision, not a saving.
terms.whyItMatters: An entertainment-marketing roleplay kills a campaign after the spokesperson signs; this clause decides whether cancelling saves the client any money at all.

terms.definition: The revenue and price premium a franchise commands beyond what its market size and won-loss record predict — the residual once those are stripped out — which is why a losing team with deep support remains worth sponsoring.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-valuation case hands you two teams with equal attendance and opposite records; the residual, not the standings, says which audience a sponsor should buy.

terms.definition: Total campaign spend divided by net new full-season accounts — net of accounts lost over the same period — and judged against each account's renewal-adjusted multi-year value rather than one season's price.
terms.whyItMatters: A ticket-marketing roleplay calls a $300 acquisition cost too high; the renewal rate across three seasons decides whether it actually is.

terms.definition: A fan base's favorability toward a brand divided by the general population's, times 100 — a score of 140 means those fans are 40% more likely to favor it, and sponsors generally want above roughly 120 before paying a premium.
terms.whyItMatters: A sponsorship-sales roleplay demands proof the audience fits; the index score is the argument for charging above the rate card.

terms.definition: The guaranteed payment buying the association itself — the right to be called an official partner and to use the marks — separate from the money spent activating it and separate from any advertising bought around the event.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges test whether you can split the three budgets; quoting one blended 'sponsorship cost' loses the point every time.

terms.definition: A measured intensity tier — avid, casual or aware — built from attendance, media consumption and merchandise spend together rather than from ticket purchases alone, because the tiers convert to sponsor and premium offers at very different rates.
terms.whyItMatters: A fan-database roleplay asks who to target for a premium package; the avidity tier, not last season's buyer list, is what converts.

terms.definition: A perimeter around a host venue, set by ordinance for a defined window of dates, inside which signage, sampling and vending by non-sponsors is prohibited — the enforcement tool that makes paid exclusivity worth anything.
terms.whyItMatters: An event-sponsorship roleplay has a rival brand sampling across the street; whether you can stop them depends on the zone's boundary and its dates.

terms.definition: A period before rights reach open bidding in which the incumbent partner may negotiate alone, often paired with a matching right afterward, so a rival's bid can be topped rather than won outright.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-rights renewal roleplay asks why a competitor never got to bid; the window and the matching right are the whole reason.
